description: Tunisian engineering students with a mission to give our best and leave the rest for fate to decide.
summary: Marsouine is a map for an astronaut walking on Mars. Stop by stop, it tells them whether the ground ahead is firm, sandy or too steep, and how sure we are. We built it for the boxwork region of Mount Sharp in Gale crater, along the route NASA's Curiosity rover drove between sols 4534 and 4805. The map combines three readings of the same ground: our own AI reading Curiosity's Navcam photos, a 1 m elevation and slope model from USGS, and a simulated scout drone for the ground between photos. From these it builds a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO map in 2D and 3D. A tablet plans the walk from A to B, and the astronaut's phone becomes a portal into the 3D terrain: walking in the room moves them on Mars, along a green route guide drawn on the ground. It matters because the first crews on Mars will walk where no rover has driven, and they need to know before each step whether the ground will hold.
details:
What it does

  • AI terrain reading: a DeepLabV3+ model we trained on the AI4Mars dataset reads Curiosity's Navcam photos at 55 boxwork stops, and finds sand, soil, bedrock and big rocks.
    • Sand IoU 0.966 and mean IoU 0.821 on the AI4Mars expert test set.
    • Result: 50 stops green, 4 orange, 1 red.
    • Rover heights match it to 0.08 m at 183 waypoints.
    • Slope classes (team assumptions): GO under 15°, caution 15–25°, NO-GO 25° or more.
    • For a crew on foot, the box is 55.7 % GO, 27.3 % caution and 16.6 % NO-GO.
    • Curiosity's own path is only 1.0 % NO-GO, so the limits are not too strict.
    • 5 routes between the stops, none crossing NO-GO.
    • A 3D viewer, a layer-by-layer animation, and an astronaut's-eye walk view in the colours of NASA's Mastcam panorama.
    • Height error 4.4 cm on the real route.
    • 95 % safe landings over 40 seeds.
    • The tablet plans A → B routes on the 2D or 3D map and pairs the helmet phone with a QR code.
    • The phone shows the helmet view, then opens a portal into the 3D terrain (WebXR AR, or compass + step counting).
    • The astronaut starts at A, green chevrons on the ground lead to B, and the tablet follows the astronaut live.

How it works: NASA, USGS and ESA data go through Python and QGIS pipelines into GeoTIFF layers and web textures. The app is React; the 3D views use three.js; a small Python server links the tablet and the phone. Every threshold the team chose is listed in ASSUMPTIONS.md in the repository.

Benefits:

  • Each GO/NO-GO decision can be traced to its source layer.
  • It says how sure it is, and marks what is real and what is simulated.
  • It runs on one laptop and a phone, with no internet.

What we hope to achieve: a planning and walking aid that crews and mission planners could use with the orbital and rover data that already exist.

Tools and languages:

  • Python (rasterio, geopandas, SciPy, scikit-image, scikit-learn), QGIS, Blender.
  • PyTorch with segmentation-models-pytorch (Google Colab).
  • JavaScript: React, Leaflet, three.js, esbuild, WebXR.
  • Hardware: a laptop and an Android phone.

Honest limits:

  • The thresholds are team assumptions, not NASA rules.
  • The AI was trained on rover images.
  • The drone and helmet sensors are simulations.
  • Absolute heights carry about ±15 m between products.
